content.thinking:
I need to frame the symptom clearly: account pages loaded slowly for shoppers, no numbers, concise. Then I'm tracing the causal chain starting with the median response time jump from baseline to during the incident, peaking at its worst point, and I need to cite the supporting data for that.

Following that, the reason behind the slowdown was that every summary cache lookup was being refused — a connection refused error to the redis cache endpoint — forcing the page to recompute the summary on every request instead of using cache, which I can confirm from the service comment explaining this fallback behavior. Digging further, that refusal traces back to a deployment that changed the cache port, which running config and replica revision data confirm was live across all replicas by the time of onset. I'm also ruling out an earlier deployment as the cause, since metrics show the service was healthy in the window between that deploy and the incident's onset, and a later rollback back to that same earlier revision is further confirmation it wasn't the culprit.

I've also ruled out any flag changes in the hour before onset. Looking closer, the actual mismatch is that the cache listens on a different port than what was configured, so when the port changed, nothing was listening there — every lookup failed, triggering the fallback to recompute every request, and the fact that rolling back to the old port restored service backs this up. Checking whether this mechanism depends on any evidence I haven't verified, it's solidly grounded in the config diff, the running service state, and the connection-refused logs, so I'm confident this reaches an actual root cause. The record doesn't explain why the port was changed in the first place, so I'll stop here rather than speculating further.

Looking at why the system let this change cause harm, there's no validation step checking the cache port before deployment, and the fallback silently degrades performance without triggering any alert on cache failures — detection only happened because of the latency spike, not a dedicated check. I'm also noting the disconnect error logs started slightly before the deploy itself, with the error rate staying flat compared to baseline, so I shouldn't overstate their relevance to the incident timeline.

Tracing the causal chain now: shoppers saw median response time jump from baseline to a much slower average, worse at peak, though failed requests stayed within normal range — citing AL1 and T5 for those figures. The root cause was the account page falling back to recomputing each summary live instead of pulling it from cache, because every cache lookup was being refused at the configured address (citing Gd3f7 and S1). And the reason lookups failed is that the running configuration pointed the service at the wrong port on the cache host, confirmed across all replicas as of the deployment revision.

Deploy P2 is what introduced this — it changed the cache.port value in the production deploy config, and rolling it back restored service, confirmed by the timeline entries. I'm ruling out the prior deploy (baseline metrics were healthy before onset and rollback confirmed), feature flag changes, and code changes, since the diff only touched the values file. The core root cause boils down to: nothing was listening on the new port, so connections were refused.

Ordering the chain now: symptom leads to recompute, which happens because lookups are refused, which happens because config points to 6380 where nothing listens, which traces to deploy P2's change — that's where ruled_out applies, and why it was changed remains unknown so I'll stop there. For contributing factors, I'm noting that nothing in review or deploy verifies the cache address in the production values file actually matches where the cache listens, so the bad config shipped unchecked.

CF-2 covers how cache failures silently degrade into slowness instead of surfacing as errors, with no alerting on lookup failures or hit ratio — the issue was only caught via a p50 latency alert that fired minutes after onset, so I'm proposing a connectivity-failure alert that could fire almost immediately instead. I'm now starting to note CF-3 around the absence of automatic rollback or post-deploy health checks.

For action items, I'm settling on a deploy-time check that verifies io-shop can reach the summary cache before rollout proceeds (answering CF-1), and a detection alert for summary cache lookup failures like connection refused (answering CF-2). I'll skip a second detection item around cache hit ratio since there's no supporting data for it, and I'm not treating "nobody was paged" as a real factor since Argus resolved it automatically within seconds.

I'm also flagging that AI-3 remains open with automatic sync still disabled, and the repository itself still has the bad port 6380 in its values file — so turning sync back on or redeploying from the repo as-is would undo Argus's manual fix and reintroduce the slow lookups.

For the lessons, what went well: Argus rolled back the change after the alert, Mitigation Agent confirmed the rollback fixed things, Investigator traced the slowdown to the port change via diff and connection logs, and Code-Fix drafted PR #365 with a test. What went wrong: nobody appears to have been paged — there's no linked on-call incident, which might be worth flagging as a gap.

For assumptions, the slowdown being caused by recomputation comes from a comment description rather than measured recompute time, the cache's health is the Investigator's unverified claim, and the listening port (6379) is inferred from the rollback recovery rather than directly observed.

I'm drafting the cause-in-plain-words statement: a configuration change pointed the shop at the wrong address for its cache, so lookups were refused and account pages had to recompute figures from scratch each time, keeping them correct but slow. I need to be careful about citing specific figures like port numbers and PR identifiers, making sure to attribute them to their proper reference labels rather than stating them as bare facts.

The symptom to record is that shoppers' account pages loaded slowly while this was happening, and I should align the timing — deploy at 17:39, onset at 17:40 — matching what the references say before I write it up.

action_items.item: Add a deploy-time check that blocks an io-shop rollout unless the service can connect to the summary cache at the configured host and port.
Add an alert on io-shop summary cache lookup failures, such as connection refused, so a broken cache address is flagged directly rather than only through latency.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly. The median time to serve a request rose from {series_before} before the onset to {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and was {series_at_worst} at its worst. Failed requests did not rise beyond their normal variation.

The account page was recomputing each shopper's summary instead of reading it from the summary cache, because every cache lookup was failing with connection refused. The running configuration says the page recomputes whenever the cache cannot be reached.

Lookups were refused because the running configuration pointed the service at port {S1.3} on the cache host, and the cache refused connections there. As of {T11.1}, all {T11.2} replicas ran revision 0d8e826, whose deploy/values-production.yaml sets that port. With the port rolled back, the service returned to normal.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision 544cef36a8eaf45c5b030c3d5c21473d8176cef3 at {P1.1}. The metrics read back show the service at its normal latency between that deploy and the onset. The confirmed rollback put that revision back and the service recovered.
A feature flag change. The flag provider showed {T17.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus in the {T17.3} hour before {T17.4}.
A change to io-shop's code. The deployment's diff modifies only deploy/values-production.yaml, and every file it does not list is as it was at the previous revision.

causal_chain.step: The deploy at {P2.1} of revision 0d8e826 changed cache.port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}. It was the only change in that deployment's diff. Rolling that deployment back was confirmed to end the incident. The record does not show why the port was changed.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A configuration change pointed the shop at the wrong door on its cache, so every cache lookup was refused and the account page had to work each shopper's figures out from scratch, which kept it correct but made it slow.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen, in review or at deploy, that the cache address in deploy/values-production.yaml points to where the cache accepts connections. That file ships as configuration without the service being rebuilt, so a wrong port does not break any build.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The port edit would have been caught before revision 0d8e826 reached production, and account pages would not have slowed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Because the page falls back to recomputing, refused cache lookups show up only as slowness, not as failed requests. No alert on cache lookup failures was seen. The fault was found only by the median latency alert, after its condition had held through the rule's wait.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: An alert on refused cache lookups, which the logs show starting at the deploy, would have flagged the fault sooner and pointed straight at the cache address.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well: Argus rolled back the deployment of io-shop {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
The Mitigation Agent confirmed, {T23.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, that the rollback had brought the service back from the incident's level.
The Investigator tied the slowdown to the port change by pairing the deployment's diff with the refused cache lookups in the logs, and checked the flag provider's history.
Code-Fix proposed a fix, with a test, as a draft pull request (T25).
went_wrong: Nobody was paged, so no person on call was told about the incident or the rollback while it ran.

input.root_cause: Revision 0d8e826 changed the summary cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, and the cache refused connections on the new port. Every cache lookup failed, so the account page fell back to recomputing each shopper's summary on every request. The page stayed correct but became slow.
input.still_at_risk: The repository's deploy/values-production.yaml still sets the cache port to {S1.3}, where lookups were refused, so syncing or deploying io-shop from the repository as it stands would put that port back and slow account pages again.
